Haughty

HAW-tee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Haughty is arrogantly proud and superior in manner or attitude.

The haughty museum donor insisted her name appear before every other patron's on the new wing's plaque, no matter their contribution.

Worked Example

Even after losing the championship, the haughty team captain refused to congratulate the winners, insisting his team was still clearly the better one.

Haughty describes an overall attitude of superiority -- it's less about one dismissive glance and more about a lasting sense that you're simply above everyone else.

How Haughty Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

arrogant

arrogant: having an exaggerated sense of one's own importance

lofty

lofty: having a sense of great superiority (a word taught elsewhere in this course)

Antonyms

humble

humble: modest, not thinking oneself superior

unpretentious

unpretentious: simple and modest, without airs

How Strong Is It? — proud → haughty → overbearing

proud vs. haughty

proud vs. haughty: Being proud can be perfectly healthy -- pride in your own accomplishments doesn't require looking down on anyone else.

overbearing vs. haughty

overbearing vs. haughty: Overbearing pushes even further than haughty, adding a controlling, domineering edge on top of the arrogance.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — haught-

root — haught-: high, lofty (Old French haut, from Latin altus)

suffix — -y

suffix — -y: having the quality of (Old English -ig)

Put it together

Put it together: Haughty comes from Old French haut ('high'), itself from Latin altus ('high'). Someone haughty holds their head high, looking down on everyone else -- a lofty attitude in the most literal sense.

Use the root in a new word: altitude

Use the root in a new word: altitude: Altitude, a measure of height, comes from the very same Latin altus ('high') that gives haughty its 'lofty' meaning.

Root Check

Word Choice

Haughty describes a person's whole bearing or personality -- a standing sense of superiority -- while its cousin supercilious (also in this unit) usually points to one scornful look or remark in the moment.
